facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
On 23 April 2012 five individuals (Mr I. Bakirov, Mr S. Davidis, Ms Y. Lukyanova, Ms N. Mityushkina and Mr S. Udaltsov) submitted notice of a public demonstration to the mayor of Moscow.
The planned march had an estimated 5,000 participants.
The planned march was to begin at 4 p.m. on 6 May 2012 from Triumfalnaya Square.
The planned march was to be followed by a meeting at Manezhnaya Square, which was to end at 8 p.m.

The aim of the demonstration was to protest against abuses and falsifications in the course of the elections to the State Duma and of the President of the Russian Federation, and to demand fair elections, respect for human rights, the rule of law and the international obligations of the Russian Federation.

On 3 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security approved the alternative route from Kaluzhskaya Square, down Bolshaya Yakimanka Street and Bolshaya Polyanka Street, followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
The march began at 4.30 p.m. at Kaluzhskaya Square.
The march proceeded down Yakimanka Street peacefully and without disruption.
The turnout at the march exceeded expectations, but there is no consensus as to the exact numbers.
At approximately 5 p.m. the march approached Bolotnaya Square.
By approximately 5 p.m. on 6 May 2012, the stage had been erected at the far end of Bolotnaya Embankment and a considerable number of people had already accumulated in front of it.

Faced with the police cordon and unable to access the park, the leaders of the march – Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin – stopped and demanded that the police open access to the park.

After around fifteen minutes of attempting to engage with the cordon officers, at 5.16 p.m. the four leaders (Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin) announced that they were going on a 'sit-down strike' and sat on the ground.
The people behind the four leaders stopped, although some people continued to go past them towards the stage.
The leaders of the sit-in called on other demonstrators to follow their example and sit down, but only a few of their entourage did so (between approximately twenty and fifty people in total).
At 5.50 p.m. the crowd around the sit-down protest built up, which caused some congestion, and the leaders abandoned the protest and headed towards the stage, followed by the crowd.
Some protesters held up metal barriers and aligned them so as to resist the police, threw various objects at the police, shouted and chanted 'Shame!' and other slogans.
At 6.20 p.m. Mr S. Udaltsov climbed onto the stage at the opposite end of the square to address the meeting.
At 6.20 p.m. many people were assembled in front of the stage, but the sound equipment had been disconnected.

Mr S. Udaltsov took a loudspeaker and addressed the crowd, calling for an indefinite protest action and stating that they would not leave until their comrades had been released, until the inauguration had been cancelled and until they were given airtime on the central television channels.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Bolotnaya Square at around 6 p.m. to take part in the meeting.
The applicant stood in front of the stage on Bolotnaya Embankment, within the area designated as the meeting venue.
According to the applicant, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. the area around him remained peaceful, although there was general confusion.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly adopted by the Venice Commission at its 83rd Plenary Session (Venice, 4 June 2010) provided that an assembly should be deemed peaceful if its organisers have professed peaceful intentions and the conduct of the assembly is non-violent, and that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
The applicant was detained at the police station for at least thirty-six hours pending administrative proceedings.

In the administrative proceedings, the applicant was found guilty of failure to obey lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.

A cordon of riot police in full protection gear barred access to the park at Bolotnaya Square and continued along the whole perimeter of the meeting area, channelling the demonstration to Bolotnaya Embankment.
Further down Bolotnaya Embankment there was a row of metal detectors at the entrance to the meeting venue.

Faced with the police cordon and unable to access the park, the leaders of the march – Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin – stopped and demanded that the police open access to the park.
The cordon officers did not enter into any discussion with the protest leaders and no senior officer was delegated to negotiate.
At approximately 5.55 p.m. a commotion arose near the police cordon at the place vacated by the sit-down protest, and the police cordon was broken in several places.
Within seconds the police restored the cordon, which was reinforced by additional riot police.
The police cordon began to push the crowd into the restricted area and advanced by several metres, pressing it inwards.
At 6 p.m. Police Colonel A. Makhonin told Ms N. Mityushkina to make an announcement from the stage that the meeting was over.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
Running in tight formations, the riot police pushed the crowd apart, arrested some people, confronted others and formed new cordons to isolate sections of the crowd.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
At 6.21 p.m. several police officers arrested Mr S. Udaltsov and took him away from the stage.
Mr A. Navalnyy attempted to go up onto the stage, but he was also arrested at the stairs and taken away.
At 6.25 p.m. the police arrested Mr B. Nemtsov, who had also attempted to address people from the stage.
At Malyy Kamennyy Bridge the police continued dividing the crowd and began pushing some sections away from the venue.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.

The applicant claimed that he had heard the police orders made through a megaphone to disperse, but in the general commotion he was unable to leave immediately and remained within the authorised meeting area until 7 p.m., when he was arbitrarily arrested by the police dispersing the demonstration.
The police apprehended the applicant and took him to a police van, where he waited for an hour before it left Bolotnaya Square for the police station.

At the Krasnoselskiy district police station an on-duty officer drew up a statement on an administrative offence on the basis of a report by Police Officer Y., who had allegedly arrested the applicant.
Police Officer Y.'s report contained a handwritten statement that on 6 May 2012 at 9.30 p.m., at 5/16 Bolotnaya Square, together with Police Lieutenant A., he arrested the applicant (Mr Frumkin).

The rest of Police Officer Y.'s report was a printed template stating that the applicant, acting in a group of citizens, took part in an authorised meeting, went out onto the road and thus obstructed the traffic, did not react to the multiple demands of the police to vacate the road, thereby disobeying a lawful order of the police, who were fulfilling their service duty of maintaining public order and ensuring safety, and thereby committed an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The statement on the administrative offence contained an identical text to the printed template but indicated that the applicant had been arrested at 8.30 p.m.
The applicant was charged with obstructing traffic and disobeying lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant's administrative detention was ordered with reference to Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The 'reasons' section of the administrative detention order remained blank.
Having spent the day in a transit van without food or drink, at 11.55 p.m. on 7 May 2012 the applicant was taken back to the cell at the Krasnoselskiy district police station.
A new order for the applicant's administrative detention was issued on 7 May 2012, indicating that he had been detained 'for the purpose of drawing up the administrative material'.

On the basis of the report written by Police Officer Y., the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka district established that at 8.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the applicant had been walking along the road at Bolotnaya Square and obstructing the traffic, and that he had then disobeyed lawful police orders to vacate the venue.

The applicant was found guilty of disobeying lawful police orders and was sentenced under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation to fifteen days' administrative detention.
The security plan was a ninety-nine-page internal document which had not been disclosed to the public or to the organisers.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to search the demonstrators to prevent them from taking camping tents to the site of the meeting.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to obstruct access to Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, diverting the marchers to Bolotnaya Embankment, the site of the meeting.
The adjacent park at Bolotnaya Square had to be cordoned off under the security plan.

The only entrance to Bolotnaya Embankment – from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge – had to be equipped with fourteen metal detectors, which were to be removed just before the march approached the site of the meeting.
The leaders of the march found that the layout of the meeting and the placement of the police cordon did not correspond to what they had anticipated.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.

After the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the Moscow Department of the Interior prepared a security plan and map providing for the park at Bolotnaya Square to be cordoned off with metal barriers and for the participants in the meeting to be accommodated on the road at Bolotnaya Embankment.

The security plan and security maps were prepared at extremely short notice (during the night of 4-5 May 2012 and the day of 5 May 2012) and were approved on 5 May 2012 by senior officials at the Moscow Department of the Interior.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that on 4 May 2012 the Moscow Department of the Interior published a plan on its website indicating that all of Bolotnaya Square, including the public gardens, would be given over to the rally, while Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge would be closed to vehicles but would remain open to pedestrians.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.

The Expert Commission's report stated that as the march approached Bolotnaya Square, demonstrators found that a police cordon was blocking off most of the square, leaving only a narrow stretch along the waterfront for the rally.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that when the march approached the venue of the meeting, they saw that the map showing where people would assemble on the square had been essentially altered, with the park at Bolotnaya Square, taking up approximately 80% of the square, barred and cordoned off.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that since the cordon did not correspond to the map, the column stopped and the event organisers and the people who came just waited for the police to remove the wrong cordon and for the police chiefs to reply as to what had changed.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the official website of the Moscow Department of the Interior published the map on which it was shown, just as agreed and just as on 4 February 2012, that the border of the meeting venue was outlined at the far end of the park and not the near one, and that all agreements were breached.
Mr B. Nemtsov testified that on the website of the Moscow Department of the Interior a map was posted showing that the park of Bolotnaya Square should have been open, but it turned out to be closed.

Mr B. Nemtsov testified that on 4 February 2012 there was an authorised event where all of Bolotnaya Square was open with no cordons on Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, and they were sure that on 6 May 2012 it would be exactly the same, but the police had blocked Bolotnaya Square leaving a very narrow passage for the demonstrators.
Ms N. Mirza testified that on 6 May 2012 she was present as an observer and that unlike the usual events held at Bolotnaya Square, the park was cordoned off.

Ms N. Mirza testified that as she was later told by Police Colonel V. Biryukov, the protesters had sat down on the ground because the passage had been narrowed down, and she confirmed that the passage was much narrower than usual and there were metal detectors which were not supposed to be there.
Mr N. Svanidze testified that he was convinced that the meeting had been authorised at Bolotnaya Square and the park at Bolotnaya Square.

The witness Mr D. Deynichenko testified that it had been discussed with the organisers how the cordon would be placed from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge to the park of Bolotnaya Square, so the organisers knew of the cordon in advance.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that no official map had been adopted with the organisers and that the published map had been based on Mr S. Udaltsov's own interview with journalists.

The witness Police Colonel Y. Zdorenko testified that following information received from undercover sources concerning the possible setting-up of a camp site, at around 9 p.m. on 5 May 2012 he arrived at Bolotnaya Square and organised a search of the area including the park, and the park was cordoned off and guarded.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that there are no grounds to consider the closure of access to the park of Bolotnaya Square and the placement of a guiding police cordon at the foot of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge to be a provocation, since it was only to indicate the direction and it did not obstruct access to the meeting venue at Bolotnaya Square.

The Federal Law on assemblies, meetings, demonstrations, marches and pickets (no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004, the Public Events Act) required that notification of a public event be filed by its organiser in writing with the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities no earlier than fifteen days and no later than ten days prior to the scheduled date of the event.

Section 8 of the Public Events Act provided that a public event may be held at any venue suitable for the purposes of the event, provided that it does not create a risk of the collapse of buildings or structures or any other threats to the safety of the participants.

Section 12(1)(iii) of the Public Events Act required the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities, upon receipt of the notification of a public event, to appoint an authorised representative to assist the event organisers in conducting the event in accordance with the law, with the appointment to be formally made by a written decision sent to the event organiser prior to the scheduled date of the event.

Section 12(1)(iv) of the Public Events Act required the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities to inform the organiser of the public event of the maximum capacity of the territory or venue where the public event is to be held.

Section 12(1)(v) of the Public Events Act required the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities to ensure, within its competence and jointly with the organiser and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, public order and the safety of citizens during the public event and, if necessary, to provide them with urgent medical aid.

Section 12(2) of the Public Events Act required the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities to immediately notify the organiser of the public event by issuing a reasoned written warning if the information in the notification gave grounds to suppose that the aims or conduct of the planned event did not comply with the Constitution of the Russian Federation or were in breach of prohibitions established by administrative or criminal legislation.

Section 13(1) of the Public Events Act provided that the representative of the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities had the right to require the organiser of a public event to comply with the conditions for holding the event and to decide on the suspension or termination of the public event.

Section 13(2) of the Public Events Act required the representative of the executive body of the constituent entity of the Russian Federation or the municipal authorities to be present at the public event, to assist the event organiser in the conduct of the public event, and to ensure, jointly with the organiser and the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior, public order and the safety of citizens and compliance with the law during the event.

Section 14(1) of the Public Events Act required the chief of the department of the interior in charge of the territory or venue where the public event is intended to be held to appoint an authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior to assist the event organiser in maintaining public order and the safety of citizens, with the appointment to be formally made by a written decision.

Section 14(2) of the Public Events Act provided that the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior had the right to require the organiser to announce the closure of access to the event if the maximum capacity of the venue is exceeded, to require the organiser and participants to comply with the conditions for holding the event, and at the request of the event organiser to remove any citizens disobeying the organiser's lawful orders.

Section 14(3) of the Public Events Act required the authorised representative of the Ministry of the Interior to facilitate the conduct of the public event and to ensure, jointly with the organiser and the executive body, public order and the safety of citizens and compliance with the law during the public event.

Section 15 of the Public Events Act provided that if during the holding of a public event there occurs, through the fault of the participants, a breach of lawful order which does not entail a risk to the life or health of the participants, the representative of the executive body may require the event organiser to remedy the breach, and if the breach is not remedied the public event shall be terminated in accordance with section 17 of the Public Events Act.

Section 16 of the Public Events Act provided that a public event may be terminated if the event has created a real danger for the life and health of citizens or for the possessions of individuals or legal persons, or if the participants have committed unlawful acts and the organisers have deliberately breached the provisions of the Public Events Act relating to the conditions for holding the event.

Section 17(1) of the Public Events Act provided that in the event that a decision to terminate a public event is taken, the authorised representative of the executive body shall order the event organiser to terminate the public event giving the justification, determine a time-limit for compliance, and if the organiser does not comply, address the participants directly and allow additional time for compliance.
Section 17(2) of the Public Events Act provided that in the event of non-compliance with the order to terminate a public event, the police shall take all necessary measures to terminate the event.

Section 17(3) of the Public Events Act provided that the procedure for termination set out in section 17(1) shall not apply if mass disorder, riots, arson attacks or other emergency situations occur, in which case the termination shall be carried out in accordance with the legislation of the Russian Federation.

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of the officer's official duties relating to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the officer's performance of his or her official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 or by administrative detention for up to fifteen days.

Article 20.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that breaches of the established procedure for the organisation of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between ten and twenty times the minimum wage payable by the organisers, and breaches of the established procedure for the conduct of such events shall be punishable by a fine of between RUB 1,000 and RUB 2,000 for the organisers and between RUB 500 and RUB 1,000 for the participants.

Article 27.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that the escorting or transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative-offence report shall be carried out as quickly as possible and shall be recorded in an escort-operation report, an administrative-offence report or an administrative-detention report.

Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that administrative detention or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed, and that where the detained person so requests, his or her family, the administrative department at the person's place of work or study and his or her defence counsel shall be informed of his or her whereabouts.

Article 27.4 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that administrative detention shall be recorded in a report, and that if the detained person so requests, he or she shall be given a copy of the administrative-detention report.

Article 27.5 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that the duration of administrative detention shall not exceed three hours, except in the cases set out in paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Article.

Article 27.5 § 3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences punishable, among other administrative sanctions, by administrative detention may be subject to administrative detention for up to forty-eight hours.

Article 27.5 § 4 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provided that the term of administrative detention shall be calculated from the time when a person escorted in accordance with Article 27.2 is taken to the police station.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that any prior restrictions should be formalised in writing and communicated to the organiser of the event within a reasonable timeframe, and that the relevant authorities must ensure that any restrictions imposed during an event are in full conformity with the law.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that any restrictions placed on an assembly should be communicated in writing to the event organiser with a brief explanation of the reason for each restriction, and that such decisions should be communicated within a reasonable timeframe sufficiently far in advance to allow judicial appeal before the notified date of the event.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement agencies should be proactive in engaging with assembly organizers, that there should be a nominated point of contact within the law enforcement agency whom protesters can contact before or during an assembly, and that the policing operation should be characterized by a policy of 'no surprises'.

The aim of the demonstration was to protest against abuses and falsifications in the course of the elections to the State Duma and of the President of the Russian Federation, and to demand fair elections, respect for human rights, the rule of law and the international obligations of the Russian Federation.

The organisers of the rejected meeting at Manezhnaya Square had expressed their intention to proceed in defiance of the ban and to occupy the square from 6 to 10 May 2012, ready to resist the police if necessary.
The Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow Department of the Interior to safeguard public order in Moscow in light of the threatened unauthorised occupation of Manezhnaya Square.
The Moscow Department of Regional Security referred to information found on the Internet that the demonstrators would go to Manezhnaya Square after the meeting.

The security plan provided for security measures in Moscow city centre in view of the forthcoming authorised demonstration at Bolotnaya Square and anticipated attempts by other opposition groups to hold unauthorised public gatherings.

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.
The security plan provided for a 350-strong police unit for intercepting and apprehending organisers and instigators of unauthorised gatherings.
If faced with an unauthorised gathering, units were instructed to give a warning through a loudspeaker, to arrest the most active participants and to record video-footage of those incidents.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to search the demonstrators to prevent them from taking camping tents to the site of the meeting.
At 5.55 p.m. the media reported that the police authorities were regarding the sit-down strike as a provocation of mass disorder and were considering prosecuting those responsible for it.
At approximately 6 p.m. a Molotov cocktail was launched from the crowd at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge over the restored police cordon.
The Molotov cocktail landed outside the cordon and the trousers of a passer-by caught fire.
Some protesters held up metal barriers and aligned them so as to resist the police, threw various objects at the police, shouted and chanted 'Shame!' and other slogans.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, at 5.04 p.m. the organised procession arrived at the police cordon and expressed the intention to proceed straight to Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge and to Borovitskaya Square.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 5.58 p.m. to 7 p.m. persons on Malyy Kamennyy Bridge and Bolotnaya Embankment made attempts to break the cordon, and threw empty glass bottles, fireworks, chunks of tarmac and portable metal barriers at the police officers.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. necessary measures were taken to push citizens away from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, Bolotnaya Embankment and Bolotnaya Street and to arrest those who resisted the most, during which twenty-eight police officers and military servicemen sustained injuries of various gravity, four of whom were hospitalised.

On 6 May 2012 the Investigative Committee of the Russian Federation opened a criminal investigation into suspected offences of mass disorder and violent acts against the police under Article 212 § 2 and Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
On 28 May 2012 an investigation was launched into the criminal offence of organising mass disorder under Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

The Expert Commission noted that the authorities received information that the protesters might attempt to establish a protest camp at the site, causing them to decide that the rally should be confined to only the Bolotnaya waterfront area – a much smaller area than had been originally allocated for the assembly.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 5.42 p.m. the chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior issued a statement characterising the organisers' refusal to proceed to the agreed place of the rally as creating a real threat of a jam and trauma for participants, and announcing that an inquiry commission was working on the spot to document actions related to appeals to commit mass public disorder.

The Investigative Committee found on 20 March 2013 that after the organisers had decided to call a sit-down protest they provoked mass disorder, during which the participants threw various objects at the police, causing injuries to some of them, and that the police officers detained those participating in the mass disorder with justifiable use of force.

The witness N. Sharapov testified that Mr S. Udaltsov had known the route of the march and had not raised a question regarding opening up the park at Bolotnaya Square, and that the park had been opened up previously as an exception on only one occasion, on 4 February 2012, because it was winter, it was snowing and the declared number of participants had significantly exceeded 5,000.

The witness M. Volondina testified that before the beginning of the march, police information came through from undercover sources that the event organisers intended to encircle the Kremlin holding hands to prevent the inauguration of the Russian President.
The witness Y. Vanyukhin testified that on 6 May 2012 at around 6 p.m. Mr S. Udaltsov, while on the way to the stage, told people around him that they were going to set up camp.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that the mass disorder organised by Mr S. Udaltsov and others led to the destabilisation of public order and peace in a public place during the conduct of a public event, put a large number of people in danger, and led to considerable psychological tension in the vicinity of Bolotnaya Square in Moscow, accompanied by violence against the police and the destruction of property.

Article 212 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that the organisation of mass disorder accompanied by violence, riots, arson, destruction of property, use of firearms, explosives and explosive devices, as well as by armed resistance to a public official, shall be punishable by four to ten years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that participation in mass disorder as provided for in Article 212 § 1 shall be punishable by three to eight years' deprivation of liberty.

Article 212 § 3 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that the instigation of mass disorder or the instigation of participation in it, or the instigation of violence against citizens, shall be punishable by restriction of liberty for up to two years, or community work for up to two years, or deprivation of liberty for the same term.

Article 318 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provided that the use of violence not endangering life or health, or the threat to use such violence, against a public official or his or her relatives in connection with the performance of his or her duties shall be punishable by a fine of up to 200,000 Russian roubles or the equivalent of the convicted person's wages for eighteen months, or community work for up to five years, or up to five years' deprivation of liberty.
At the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the organisers stated that the turnout could significantly exceed the expected 5,000 participants.
At the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the organisers were warned that exceeding the number originally declared would be unacceptable.

According to the applicant, during the working meeting on 4 May 2012 the organisers and the authorities agreed that, since there was insufficient time for an on-the-spot reconnaissance, the assembly layout and the security arrangements would be identical to the previous public event organised by the same group of opposition activists on 4 February 2012.
On 4 February 2012, the previous public event had proceeded with a march down Yakimanka Street followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
On 4 February 2012, the venue of the meeting had included the park at Bolotnaya Square (in some documents referred to as 'Repin Park') and the Bolotnaya Embankment.
On 4 May 2012 the deputy mayor of Moscow, Mr A. Gorbenko, instructed the Tsentralnyy district prefect to assist the organisers in maintaining public order and security during the event.

On 4 May 2012 the deputy mayor of Moscow, Mr A. Gorbenko, ordered the Moscow Department of Regional Security to inform the organisers that their assembly notice had been accepted and to monitor its implementation.
Other public agencies were assigned the duties of street cleaning, traffic control and ensuring the presence of ambulances at the site of the assembly on 6 May 2012.
On 5 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow City Prosecutor's Office to issue a warning to the organisers against exceeding the notified number of participants.

On 5 May 2012 the Moscow Department of Regional Security requested the Moscow City Prosecutor's Office to issue a warning to the organisers against erecting camping tents at the meeting venue, an intention allegedly expressed by the organisers at the working meeting.

On 5 May 2012 the Tsentralnyy district prosecutor's office issued a warning to two of the organisers, Mr S. Davidis and Mr S. Udaltsov, against exceeding the notified number of participants and against erecting camping tents at the meeting venue.
On 5 May 2012 the Moscow Department of the Interior published on its website official information concerning the forthcoming demonstration on 6 May 2012, including a map.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 indicated the route of the march, the traffic restrictions and an access plan to Bolotnaya Square.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 delineated the area allotted to the meeting, which included the park at Bolotnaya Square.
The map published by the Moscow Department of the Interior on 5 May 2012 marked access to the meeting through the park at Bolotnaya Square.
On 5 May 2012 the Police Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Golovanov, adopted a plan for safeguarding public order in Moscow on 6 May 2012 (the security plan).
The security plan was a ninety-nine-page internal document which had not been disclosed to the public or to the organisers.

The security plan provided for security measures in Moscow city centre in view of the forthcoming authorised demonstration at Bolotnaya Square and anticipated attempts by other opposition groups to hold unauthorised public gatherings.
The security plan set up operational headquarters to implement the security measures.
Thirty-two high-ranking police officers, including eight major-generals, two military commanders and one emergency-relief official, were appointed to the operational headquarters.
The Deputy Police Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Kozlov, was appointed as head of the operational headquarters.
The Chief of the Special-Purpose Operational Centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Khaustov, was appointed as deputy head of the operational headquarters.
The Deputy Chief of the Public Order Directorate of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Colonel D. Deynichenko, was appointed as deputy head of the operational headquarters.

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.
The main contingent of the security plan was the police squad charged with cordon and riot-control duties in accordance with a structured and detailed action plan for each operational unit.

The security plan provided for a 785-strong police unit assigned to operational posts across the city centre, with responsibility for apprehending offenders, escorting them to police stations and drawing up administrative-offence reports.
The 785-strong police unit was instructed to prepare templates for the administrative-offence reports and to have at least forty printed copies of them at every police station.
The security plan provided for a 350-strong police unit for intercepting and apprehending organisers and instigators of unauthorised gatherings.
The 350-strong police unit had to be equipped with full protection gear and police batons.
Each unit in the security plan had to ensure effective radio communication within the chain of command.
Units were instructed to keep loudspeakers, metal detectors, handcuffs, fire extinguishers and wire clippers in the police vehicles.

The security plan set out in detail the allocation and deployment of police vehicles, police buses, interception and monitoring vehicles and equipment, dog-handling teams, fire-fighting and rescue equipment, ambulances and a helicopter.

The security plan made provision for a 1,815-strong reserve unit equipped with gas masks, aerosol grenades (Дрейф), flash grenades (Заря-2), bang grenades (Факел and Факел-C), a 40-mm hand-held grenade launcher (Гвоздь 6Г-30), and a 43-mm hand-held grenade launcher (ГМ-94).
The 1,815-strong reserve unit was also equipped with tubeless pistols (ПБ-4СП) with 23-mm rubber bullets and propelling cartridges, and rifles (KC-23).
Two water-cannon vehicles were ordered to be on standby, ready to be used against persistent offenders.

All units were instructed to be vigilant and thorough in detecting and eliminating security threats and to be polite and tactful in their conduct vis-à-vis citizens, engaging in lawful dialogue with them without responding to provocations.
If faced with an unauthorised gathering, units were instructed to give a warning through a loudspeaker, to arrest the most active participants and to record video-footage of those incidents.

Police chiefs were instructed to place plain-clothes officers among the protesters in order to monitor the threat of violence and terrorist attacks within the crowd and to take measures, where appropriate, to prevent and mitigate the damage and to pursue the perpetrators.

The Chief of the Tsentralnyy district of Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Paukov, was required to prepare, together with the organisers, the text of the public announcement to be made if the situation deteriorated.
The head of the press communication service of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Internal Service Lieutenant-Colonel Y. Alekseyeva, was in charge of communication with the press.

The head of the Department for Liaison with Civil Society of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Internal Service Colonel V. Biryukov, had to ensure coordination with the representatives of public organisations and coordination and information flow with other services of the Moscow Department of the Interior.
The units assigned to police the march and the meeting belonged to Zone no. 8, covering Kaluzhskaya Square, Bolotnaya Square and the adjacent territory.
The zone commander of Zone no. 8 was the Chief of the Riot Police of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Colonel P. Smirnov.

Police Colonels P. Saprykin, Y. Zdorenko, A. Kuznetsov, V. Yermakov, A. Kasatkin, A. Dvoynos, Police Lieutenant-Colonel A. Tsukernik, Police Captain R. Bautdinov and Internal Service Lieutenant-Colonel D. Bystrikov were appointed as deputy commanders of Zone no. 8.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 comprised 2,400 riot police officers, of whom 1,158 were on duty at Bolotnaya Square.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to search the demonstrators to prevent them from taking camping tents to the site of the meeting.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to obstruct access to Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, diverting the marchers to Bolotnaya Embankment, the site of the meeting.
The adjacent park at Bolotnaya Square had to be cordoned off under the security plan.

The only entrance to Bolotnaya Embankment – from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge – had to be equipped with fourteen metal detectors, which were to be removed just before the march approached the site of the meeting.
An exception was made for the organisers and the technical staff, who were allowed access behind the stage through two additional metal detectors.
Further arrangements were made for access of the press to the meeting venue.

The command of Zone no. 8, in particular Police Colonels Smirnov and Saprykin, were under orders to meet the organisers in person at the beginning of the event to remind them of their responsibilities and to have them sign an undertaking.

The organisers were to undertake to ensure the lawful and safe conduct of the event, and to refrain from any calls for forced change of the constitutional order and from hate speech and propaganda in favour of violence or war.
The organisers were to undertake to be present at the venue until the end of the assembly and the departure of the participants.
A video-recording of the briefing and the signing of the undertaking had to be made.
At approximately 1.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the organisers were allowed access to Bolotnaya Square to set up the stage and sound equipment.
The police searched the vehicles delivering the equipment and seized three tents found amid the gear.
The police arrested several people for bringing the tents to Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
The installation of the stage and sound equipment was delayed due to the police searches and arrests.
During the time of the equipment installation, communication between the organisers setting up the stage and those leading the march was sporadic.

At the beginning of the march, Police Colonel A. Makhonin met the organisers at Kaluzhskaya Square to clarify any outstanding organisational matters and to have them sign the undertaking to ensure public order during the demonstration.

Police Colonel A. Makhonin specifically asked Mr S. Udaltsov to ensure that no tents were placed on Bolotnaya Square and that the participants complied with the limits on the place and time allocated for the assembly.

The organisers gave their assurances that no tents would be placed on Bolotnaya Square and that participants would comply with the limits on the place and time allocated for the assembly, and signed the undertaking.
The march began at 4.30 p.m. at Kaluzhskaya Square.
The march proceeded down Yakimanka Street peacefully and without disruption.
The turnout at the march exceeded expectations, but there is no consensus as to the exact numbers.
The official estimate was that there were 8,000 participants in the march.
The organisers considered that there had been about 25,000 participants in the march.
The media reported different numbers of participants, some significantly exceeding the official and organisers' estimates.
At approximately 5 p.m. the march approached Bolotnaya Square.
The leaders of the march found that the layout of the meeting and the placement of the police cordon did not correspond to what they had anticipated.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.

A cordon of riot police in full protection gear barred access to the park at Bolotnaya Square and continued along the whole perimeter of the meeting area, channelling the demonstration to Bolotnaya Embankment.
Further down Bolotnaya Embankment there was a row of metal detectors at the entrance to the meeting venue.
By approximately 5 p.m. on 6 May 2012, the stage had been erected at the far end of Bolotnaya Embankment and a considerable number of people had already accumulated in front of it.

Faced with the police cordon and unable to access the park, the leaders of the march – Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin – stopped and demanded that the police open access to the park.

According to the protesters, they were taken aback by the alteration of the expected layout and demanded that the police officers at the cordon move the cordon back to allow sufficient space for the protesters to pass and to assemble for the meeting.

According to the official version, the protesters were not interested in proceeding to the meeting venue; they stopped because they had either intended to break the cordon in order to proceed towards Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge and then to the Kremlin, or to stir up the crowd to incite disorder.
The cordon officers did not enter into any discussion with the protest leaders and no senior officer was delegated to negotiate.

After around fifteen minutes of attempting to engage with the cordon officers, at 5.16 p.m. the four leaders (Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr I. Yashin) announced that they were going on a 'sit-down strike' and sat on the ground.
The people behind the four leaders stopped, although some people continued to go past them towards the stage.
The leaders of the sit-in called on other demonstrators to follow their example and sit down, but only a few of their entourage did so (between approximately twenty and fifty people in total).

Between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m. two State Duma deputies, Mr G. Gudkov and Mr D. Gudkov, contacted unidentified senior police officers to negotiate the enlargement of the restricted area by moving the police cordon behind the park along the lines expected by the organisers.

Mr V. Lukin, the Ombudsman of the Russian Federation, at the request of Police Colonel V. Biryukov, attempted to convince the leaders of the sit-in to resume the procession and to head towards the meeting venue at Bolotnaya Embankment, where the stage had been set up.

During the period between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m., no senior police officers or municipal officials came to the site of the sit-down protest, and there was no direct communication between the authorities and the leaders of the sit-in.
At 5.40 p.m. one of the meeting participants announced from the stage that the leaders were calling on the demonstrators to support their protest.
Some people waiting in front of the stage headed back to Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, either to support the sit-down protest or to leave the meeting.
The area in front of the stage almost emptied after the announcement at 5.40 p.m.

At 5.43 p.m. the media reported that Mr S. Udaltsov had demanded that the protesters be given airtime on Russia's main television channels, that the presidential inauguration of Mr Putin be cancelled and that new elections be called.
At 5.50 p.m. the crowd around the sit-down protest built up, which caused some congestion, and the leaders abandoned the protest and headed towards the stage, followed by the crowd.
At 5.55 p.m. the media reported that the police authorities were regarding the sit-down strike as a provocation of mass disorder and were considering prosecuting those responsible for it.
At approximately 5.55 p.m. a commotion arose near the police cordon at the place vacated by the sit-down protest, and the police cordon was broken in several places.
A crowd of around a hundred people spilled over to the empty space beyond the cordon after it was broken.
Within seconds the police restored the cordon, which was reinforced by additional riot police.
Those who found themselves outside the cordon wandered around, uncertain what to do next.
Several people were apprehended, others were pushed back inside the cordon, and some continued to loiter outside or walked towards the park.
The police cordon began to push the crowd into the restricted area and advanced by several metres, pressing it inwards.
At 6 p.m. Police Colonel A. Makhonin told Ms N. Mityushkina to make an announcement from the stage that the meeting was over.

Ms N. Mityushkina made the announcement from the stage that the meeting was over, but apparently her message was not heard by most of the demonstrators or the media reporters broadcasting from the spot.
The live television footage provided by the parties contained no mention of Ms N. Mityushkina's announcement that the meeting was over.
At approximately 6 p.m. a Molotov cocktail was launched from the crowd at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge over the restored police cordon.
The Molotov cocktail landed outside the cordon and the trousers of a passer-by caught fire.
The fire caused by the Molotov cocktail was promptly extinguished by the police.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
Running in tight formations, the riot police pushed the crowd apart, arrested some people, confronted others and formed new cordons to isolate sections of the crowd.
Some protesters held up metal barriers and aligned them so as to resist the police, threw various objects at the police, shouted and chanted 'Shame!' and other slogans.
Whenever the police apprehended anyone from among the protesters, other protesters attempted to pull them back.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
At 6.20 p.m. Mr S. Udaltsov climbed onto the stage at the opposite end of the square to address the meeting.
At 6.20 p.m. many people were assembled in front of the stage, but the sound equipment had been disconnected.

Mr S. Udaltsov took a loudspeaker and addressed the crowd, calling for an indefinite protest action and stating that they would not leave until their comrades had been released, until the inauguration had been cancelled and until they were given airtime on the central television channels.
At 6.21 p.m. several police officers arrested Mr S. Udaltsov and took him away from the stage.
Mr A. Navalnyy attempted to go up onto the stage, but he was also arrested at the stairs and taken away.
As Mr A. Navalnyy was pushed out by the police officers he turned to the crowd shouting 'Nobody leave!'
At 6.25 p.m. the police arrested Mr B. Nemtsov, who had also attempted to address people from the stage.
At Malyy Kamennyy Bridge the police continued dividing the crowd and began pushing some sections away from the venue.
Through the loudspeakers the police requested that the participants leave for the metro station.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.
On 6 May 2012 Police Colonel D. Deynichenko drew up a report summarising the security measures taken on that day in Moscow.
The report by Police Colonel D. Deynichenko stated that the march, in which around 8,000 people had participated, had begun at 4.15 p.m. and had followed the route to Bolotnaya Square.

The report by Police Colonel D. Deynichenko listed the groups and organisations represented at the march, the number of participants in each group, the number and colours of their flags and the number and content of their banners.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, at 5.04 p.m. the organised procession arrived at the police cordon and expressed the intention to proceed straight to Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge and to Borovitskaya Square.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, the leaders at the head of the procession – Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr A. Navalnyy – called on the marchers through the loudspeaker not to move, and together with some thirty protesters sat on the ground.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, the police repeatedly warned those sitting on the ground against holding an unauthorised public gathering and required them to proceed to the venue of the meeting or to leave.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, two State Duma deputies (Mr G. Gudkov and Mr D. Gudkov), the Ombudsman of the Russian Federation (Mr V. Lukin), and a member of the Civic Chamber (Mr N. Svanidze) talked to those sitting on the ground, but they did not react and continued chanting slogans.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 5.58 p.m. to 7 p.m. persons on Malyy Kamennyy Bridge and Bolotnaya Embankment made attempts to break the cordon, and threw empty glass bottles, fireworks, chunks of tarmac and portable metal barriers at the police officers.
According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, at 6 p.m. one of the organisers, Ms N. Mityushkina, went on the stage and declared the meeting over.
According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, at 6.20 p.m. Mr S. Udaltsov went on the stage and called on the people to take part in an indefinite protest action.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, at 7 p.m. a group of around twenty individuals including Ms N. Mityushkina attempted to put up three one-person camping tents on Bolotnaya Embankment.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. necessary measures were taken to push citizens away from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, Bolotnaya Embankment and Bolotnaya Street and to arrest those who resisted the most, during which twenty-eight police officers and military servicemen sustained injuries of various gravity, four of whom were hospitalised.
According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, in total 656 people were detained in Moscow to prevent public disorder and unauthorised demonstrations.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, the total number of troops deployed for public order and security duties in Moscow was 12,759 servicemen, including 7,609 police officers, 100 traffic police officers, 4,650 military servicemen and 400 members of voluntary brigades.

On 4 May 2012 a working meeting took place at the Moscow Department of Regional Security with participants from among the organisers and the Moscow Department of the Interior, where they discussed the arrangements for the march, the placement of metal detectors, the stage set-up and other organisational matters.

After the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the Moscow Department of the Interior prepared a security plan and map providing for the park at Bolotnaya Square to be cordoned off with metal barriers and for the participants in the meeting to be accommodated on the road at Bolotnaya Embankment.

The security plan and security maps were prepared at extremely short notice (during the night of 4-5 May 2012 and the day of 5 May 2012) and were approved on 5 May 2012 by senior officials at the Moscow Department of the Interior.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.
The Expert Commission noted that the Moscow Department of Regional Security announced on 4 May 2012 that the event would follow a similar route to the previous rally on 4 February 2012.
The Expert Commission noted that the official notification of approval for the 6 May 2012 assembly was issued on 4 May 2012 – just two days before the beginning of the event.

The Expert Commission noted that on 4 May 2012 the Moscow Department of the Interior published a plan on its website indicating that all of Bolotnaya Square, including the public gardens, would be given over to the rally, while Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge would be closed to vehicles but would remain open to pedestrians.

The Expert Commission noted that the procedure of opening all of Bolotnaya Square including the public gardens was the same procedure the authorities had adopted for the two previous rallies on Bolotnaya Square on 10 December 2011 and 4 February 2012.

The Expert Commission noted that on the evening of 5 May 2012 the police cordoned off the public gardens at Bolotnaya Square, according to Police Colonel Y. Zdorenko, in order to prevent the participants from setting up camp and from other illegal acts.

The Expert Commission noted that the authorities received information that the protesters might attempt to establish a protest camp at the site, causing them to decide that the rally should be confined to only the Bolotnaya waterfront area – a much smaller area than had been originally allocated for the assembly.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.
The Expert Commission noted that the City Council of Moscow did not send out a written announcement that a special representative from the city authorities would be present at the event.

The Expert Commission noted that the chairman of the Moscow local department of the Ministry of the Interior, Mr V. Kolokoltsev, did not issue any special orders on sending a special representative of the Ministry to the event.

The Expert Commission noted that the organisers requested twelve hours to set up a stage and sound equipment for the rally, but on the morning of 6 May 2012 the authorities only allocated six hours of advance access.

The Expert Commission noted that at 1.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the police did not allow vehicles with stage equipment onto the site until they had been searched, and the searches revealed a small number of tents, resulting in the detention of a number of people.
The Expert Commission noted that the police finally allowed the truck with the stage equipment onto Bolotnaya Square at 2.50 p.m. on 6 May 2012, just 70 minutes before the march was due to begin.

The Expert Commission's report stated that as the march approached Bolotnaya Square, demonstrators found that a police cordon was blocking off most of the square, leaving only a narrow stretch along the waterfront for the rally.
The Expert Commission's report stated that the police established a triple cordon of officers on Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, which prevented any movement in the direction of the Kremlin.

The Expert Commission's report stated that the first cordon was positioned close to the junction of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge and the Bolotnaya waterfront, comprising students from the Police College and officers of the Patrol Guard Service without any protective equipment.

The Expert Commission's report stated that behind the first cordon were two rows of OMON riot police, a line of voluntary citizen patrol ('druzhinniki'), and another cordon of OMON, with a number of water cannons visible between the second and third cordons.

The Expert Commission's report contained two photographs comparing the police cordon on 4 February 2012 (a thin line of police officers without protection gear) and the one on 6 May 2012 (multiple ranks of riot police with full protection gear backed up by heavy vehicles).

The Expert Commission's report stated that by 5.15 p.m. the majority of the march was immobile, and a number of leaders including Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy and Mr I. Yashin encouraged demonstrators to sit down on the road in front of the 'Udarnik' cinema facing the police cordon.

The Expert Commission's report stated that an estimated 50-200 people joined the sit-down protest, and the leaders stressed the need to maintain a peaceful protest and appealed to demonstrators to remain calm.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 5.42 p.m. the chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior issued a statement characterising the organisers' refusal to proceed to the agreed place of the rally as creating a real threat of a jam and trauma for participants, and announcing that an inquiry commission was working on the spot to document actions related to appeals to commit mass public disorder.

The Expert Commission's report stated that some demonstrators tried to pass through the police cordon to leave the area, but the police refused to let them through and directed them to go back through the crowd to Bolshaya Polyanka Street, even though this was practically impossible.

The Expert Commission's report stated that the police used loudspeakers to inform demonstrators of the rally location and asked participants to pass directly to Bolotnaya Square, but given the poor quality of the sound equipment, only those nearest the police could hear this information.

The Expert Commission's report stated that from the moment difficulties first arose for demonstrators attempting to cross Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, demonstrators made repeated attempts to negotiate with the police over moving their cordons to allow protesters onto Bolotnaya Square.

The Expert Commission's report stated that Mr D. Oreshkin, a member of the Presidential Human Rights Council, and State Duma deputy Mr G. Gudkov tried to talk to the police authorities at around 5.30 p.m., but there was no response.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 7.00 p.m. State Duma deputy Mr I. Ponomarev tried to stop violence during the clashes on the embankment by speaking to the authorities, but he did not get a positive response.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Ms N. Mityushkina as stating that she tried unsuccessfully to find the responsible people in the Ministry of the Interior to solve organisational problems, and that only at 6.00-6.30 p.m. did a senior police officer approach her and tell her that the authorities had suspended the demonstration and ask her to announce from the stage that the event was over.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr I. Bakirov as stating that a police officer in a colonel's uniform contacted him only once, and that later when clashes with the police erupted he could not find anyone with whom to communicate and cooperate.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr S. Davidis as stating that he personally did not meet nor have time to get into contact with the authorities regarding the fences set up around the perimeter of the rally, and that he only saw OMON officers who behaved aggressively and were not predisposed to get into a conversation.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 5.55 p.m. as people tried to move through the narrow gap between the police cordon and the waterfront, the police line moved two steps forward, further pressing the crowd, which generated a counter response from the crowd, and in several places the police cordon broke.

The Expert Commission's report stated that it was impossible to determine whether the breaking of the cordon was the result of conscious action by sections of the crowd or if the police cordon simply broke due to the pressure from such a large number of people.

The Expert Commission's report stated that just after the breaking of the police cordon at approximately 6.00 p.m., a single Molotov cocktail was thrown from the crowd, landed behind the police ranks and ignited the trousers of a 74-year-old demonstrator who had passed through the cordon, and the police used their fire extinguishers to put out the fire.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at 6.10 p.m. Mr S. Udaltsov, Mr A. Navalnyy and Mr B. Nemtsov managed to walk from the Udarnik cinema to the stage at the waterfront followed by a large number of people, and that OMON officers then detained Mr S. Udaltsov on stage and shortly afterwards detained Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr A. Navalnyy as well.

The Expert Commission's report stated that in the two hours between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. there does not appear to have been any clear reason for the police decision to advance other than to divide the crowd up into smaller sections, and that there is little evidence that demonstrators initiated the violence.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at around 6.20 p.m. the police announced that the rally was cancelled and asked protesters to disperse, but the announcement was not loud enough to reach the majority of the crowd.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at the same time as the dispersal announcement, Police Colonel V. Biryukov, head of the Moscow Department of the Interior's press service, told a group of human rights defenders that the demonstrators could continue to Bolotnaya Square to take part in the rally.
The Expert Commission's report stated that by 6.30 p.m. the crowd at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge and the waterfront was cut in two.

The Expert Commission's report stated that around 6.54 p.m. the police cordon that acted as a barrier along the waterfront near Luzhkov Bridge was removed, and demonstrators were able to move freely along the Bolotnaya waterfront.

The Expert Commission's report stated that approximately 15 minutes after 6.54 p.m., some 200 police officers in protective equipment began pushing protesters in the direction of Lavrushinsky Lane and back along the Bolotnaya waterfront from Luzhkov Bridge towards the Udarnik cinema.
The Expert Commission's report stated that at around 7.47 p.m. authorities created a corridor to allow demonstrators to leave the Bolotnaya area.
The Expert Commission's report stated that at 7.53 p.m. a group of OMON officers appeared from the bushes of Bolotnaya Gardens and divided those demonstrators that remained on the square.
The Expert Commission's report stated that at 8.08 p.m. the last groups of people slowly left the waterfront along a corridor formed by the policemen.

The Expert Commission's report stated that between 9.00 and 10.00 p.m. around two thousand demonstrators moved along Bolshaya Ordynka Street chanting slogans and OMON officers began to detain people and actively disperse the column.

On 20 March 2013 the Zamoskvoretskiy branch of the Investigative Committee dismissed ten individual complaints and two official enquiries made in relation to the allegedly unlawful acts of the police in dispersing the rally on 6 May 2012, including excessive use of force and arbitrary arrests.
The two official enquiries dismissed on 20 March 2013 were made by Mr I. Ponomarev, a deputy of the State Duma, and Mr A. Babushkin, President of the Public Supervisory Committee of Moscow.

The Investigative Committee interviewed one of the ten individuals who had lodged the complaints and four police officers deployed in the cordon around Bolotnaya Square, including squadron and regiment commanders.

The police officers stated that they had been acting under orders to maintain public safety and to identify and arrest the most active instigators of unrest, and that only those resisting the demands of the police had been arrested and no force had been used unnecessarily.
The police officers stated that when the police had had to intervene, they had used combat manoeuvres and truncheons but not tear gas or other exceptional means of restraint.
Squadron Commander S. explained that he had been deployed in the sector adjacent to the stage and that there had been no incidents or disorder in that sector and no one had been arrested.

The decision of 20 March 2013 listed thirteen other internal inquiries carried out following individual complaints and medical reports; in six cases the allegations of abuse had been found to be unsubstantiated and in seven cases the police conduct had been found to be lawful.

The Investigative Committee found on 20 March 2013 that after the organisers had decided to call a sit-down protest they provoked mass disorder, during which the participants threw various objects at the police, causing injuries to some of them, and that the police officers detained those participating in the mass disorder with justifiable use of force.
The Investigative Committee refused on 20 March 2013 to institute criminal proceedings against the police officers for the absence of corpus delicti.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that the political organisers and the formal organisers all had a clear idea that the march would follow the same route as the one that had taken place on 4 February 2012, as confirmed by the Moscow mayor's office.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that two days beforehand maps showing where people would assemble and the route of the march were published on the official news website RiaNovosti and on the police website 'Petrovka, 38'.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that when the march approached the venue of the meeting, they saw that the map showing where people would assemble on the square had been essentially altered, with the park at Bolotnaya Square, taking up approximately 80% of the square, barred and cordoned off.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that since the cordon did not correspond to the map, the column stopped and the event organisers and the people who came just waited for the police to remove the wrong cordon and for the police chiefs to reply as to what had changed.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that to show visually that they were not going anywhere, the leaders sat on the ground, and that the first line of the police cordon was composed of 20-year-old conscripts and with a thousand people pressing on it the cordon broke.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that no authorities were present on the spot and it was impossible to understand who was in command, and that State Duma deputies present on the spot tried to act as negotiators but said that nobody wanted to come up to them.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that when he was in the detention facility he lodged a complaint concerning the hindrance of a peaceful public event with the Moscow Department of the Interior, setting out arguments that officials of the Moscow Department of the Interior had deliberately provoked the crowd to panic so that they could later make claims regarding mass disorder.
On 2 December 2013 Mr S. Davidis gave testimony as a witness in the first Bolotnaya case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the negotiations with the mayor's office were very difficult this time and that it was only on 4 May 2012 that the organisers received the written agreement, with practically twenty-four hours' notice.
Mr S. Davidis testified that the organisers could not bring the vehicles carrying the stage to the square before 1 p.m. on 6 May 2012 and only had three hours to put up the stage.

Mr S. Davidis testified that at the working meeting on 4 May 2012, because there was no time for an on-site reconnaissance, at Mr D. Deynichenko's suggestion it was stated that in organising the event they would follow the example of the assembly held on 4 February 2012.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the only thing noted at the working meeting was that the stage would be a bit closer to the park at Bolotnaya Square, at the corner of the square, because originally it had been declared that there would be 5,000 participants.

Mr S. Davidis testified that when he called Mr D. Deynichenko the following day, Mr Deynichenko told him that he had had a map drawn up by the Department of the Interior and that Mr S. Udaltsov could come during the day to see it, but Mr Deynichenko postponed the meeting several times and then no longer answered the phone.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the closure of the park was not discussed at the working meeting on 4 May 2012, and that it was expressly stated that everything except the position of the stage would be the same as on 4 February 2012.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the official website of the Moscow Department of the Interior published the map on which it was shown, just as agreed and just as on 4 February 2012, that the border of the meeting venue was outlined at the far end of the park and not the near one, and that all agreements were breached.

Mr S. Davidis testified that when the emergency occurred he called Mr S. Udaltsov to tell him that the police were trying to terminate the meeting, but Mr Udaltsov replied that they were already heading to the stage and had ended the sit-in protest.
Mr S. Davidis testified that the police officers did not answer phone calls and he did not manage to find anyone in charge of the police.
On 5 December 2013 Mr B. Nemtsov gave testimony as a witness in the first Bolotnaya case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
Mr B. Nemtsov testified that on the website of the Moscow Department of the Interior a map was posted showing that the park of Bolotnaya Square should have been open, but it turned out to be closed.

Mr B. Nemtsov testified that on 4 February 2012 there was an authorised event where all of Bolotnaya Square was open with no cordons on Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, and they were sure that on 6 May 2012 it would be exactly the same, but the police had blocked Bolotnaya Square leaving a very narrow passage for the demonstrators.

Mr B. Nemtsov testified that they sat on the ground to show the police that they were not going to storm the Kremlin and Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, and that State Duma deputy Mr G. Gudkov offered to be an intermediary in the negotiations between the protesters and the police but his attempts to negotiate came to nothing.

Mr B. Nemtsov testified that when he arrived at the stage the microphones had all been switched off, Mr A. Navalnyy and Mr S. Udaltsov had been arrested just before him, and within a few minutes of taking a megaphone and addressing the people the police apprehended him.

Mr B. Nemtsov testified that the demonstration took place just one day before Mr Putin's inauguration and that the fact that the authorities had breached the agreement and closed off the square proved that there were political orders.
On 18 December 2013 Ms N. Mirza, the head of the Ombudsman's secretariat, gave testimony as a witness in the first Bolotnaya case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.
Ms N. Mirza testified that on 6 May 2012 she was present as an observer and that unlike the usual events held at Bolotnaya Square, the park was cordoned off.

Ms N. Mirza testified that Police Colonel V. Biryukov called and asked her and the Ombudsman to return urgently to Malyy Kamennyy Bridge where protesters had sat down on the ground, and that the Ombudsman tried to persuade these people to stand up and go and conduct the meeting.

Ms N. Mirza testified that the second riot police cordon, which had stood between Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge and Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, apparently approached the crowd, therefore the pressure built up from both sides.
Ms N. Mirza testified that she tried to leave the congested area and showed her observer's badge but the riot police would not listen to her and continued to press, without reacting.
Ms N. Mirza testified that Police Colonel V. Biryukov told her that he could do nothing, that he was not in charge of the riot police and that the riot police reported to the federal police.

Ms N. Mirza testified that as she was later told by Police Colonel V. Biryukov, the protesters had sat down on the ground because the passage had been narrowed down, and she confirmed that the passage was much narrower than usual and there were metal detectors which were not supposed to be there.
Ms N. Mirza testified that after the cordon had already been broken and the arrests had begun, she heard through a megaphone that the meeting was over and that people should disperse.

On 23 December 2013 Mr N. Svanidze, a member of the Civic Chamber of the Russian Federation, gave testimony as a witness in the first Bolotnaya case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.

Mr N. Svanidze testified that on 6 May 2012 he was present as an observer and that when everybody headed towards the narrow bottleneck at the embankment it created a jam, several dozen people sat on the ground, and the cordon moved towards them.

Mr N. Svanidze testified that he asked why the passage would not be opened, but Police Colonel V. Biryukov kept turning his face away and would not answer, and Mr Svanidze understood that there was no point talking to him as he was not in command.
Mr N. Svanidze testified that neither the Ombudsman nor anyone else was able to get the passage widened despite requesting it.
Mr N. Svanidze testified that there were no calls to move towards the Kremlin during the event.
Mr N. Svanidze testified that he was convinced that the meeting had been authorised at Bolotnaya Square and the park at Bolotnaya Square.
On 23 December 2013 Mr Vasilyev, a staff member at the Ombudsman's office, gave testimony as a witness in the first Bolotnaya case before the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow.

Mr Vasilyev testified that on 6 May 2012 he was present as an observer and that on that day they gathered at the press centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior, were given maps, instructions on how to behave, and the list of public observers.
Mr Vasilyev testified that the Ombudsman asked the protesters sitting on the ground why they were not going to the meeting venue, and after they got up and headed on, congestion occurred.

Mr Vasilyev testified that the Ombudsman told Police Colonel V. Biryukov to let the cordon be moved back so that people could pass, but Police Colonel V. Biryukov told him that it was outside his powers and that he did not know in whose powers it was, at which point the police began breaking the crowd up.

On 21 February 2014 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow delivered a judgment in the first Bolotnaya case finding eight individuals guilty of participation in mass disorder and of violent acts against police officers during the public assembly on 6 May 2012.
The eight individuals found guilty in the first Bolotnaya case received prison sentences of between two and a half and four years; one of them was released on parole.
Three co-defendants in the first Bolotnaya case had previously been pardoned under the Amnesty Act and a fourth had his case disjoined from the main proceedings.

On 22 May 2014 the Zamoskvoretskiy branch of the Investigative Committee dismissed five complaints by individuals who had sustained injuries on 6 May 2012, allegedly through the excessive use of force by the police.
The five complaints dismissed on 22 May 2014 had originally been a part of the criminal investigation file concerning the mass disorder at Bolotnaya Square, but were subsequently disjoined from it.
