During the investigation of the mass-disorder case, confrontations were conducted between those who had lodged complaints (in the capacity of the accused in the criminal case) and the police officers accused of violence (in the capacity of victims in the criminal case).

The Investigative Committee found on 22 May 2014 that in suppressing attempts to break the police cordon, the police officers acted in coordination and concert, without applying physical force or special means of restraint, except that the work of the officers charged with apprehending offenders did involve physical force and special means of restraint in so far as necessary against those resisting.

The Investigative Committee found on 22 May 2014 that the police officers justifiably used physical force to apprehend the participants in the mass disorder, and also special means of restraint in relation to some of them who attempted to resist.
On 20 June 2014 the Moscow City Court upheld the judgment of 21 February 2014 in the first Bolotnaya case, having slightly reduced the prison sentences for two of the defendants.
On 24 July 2014 the Moscow City Court found Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev guilty of organising mass disorder on 6 May 2012.

Udaltsov regarding the intention to proceed towards the Kremlin and to cause mass disorder.

The witness Mr A. Makhonin testified that he arrived at Bolotnaya Square after the mass disorder had already begun, and that after the mass disorder began he tried calling Mr S. Udaltsov on the phone but there was no reply.

The witness Mr A. Makhonin testified that Ms N. Mityushkina, at his request, announced the end of the meeting, and the police opened additional exits for those willing to leave and repeated through a loudspeaker the announcement of the end of the meeting.

The witness Police Colonel Y. Zdorenko testified that following information received from undercover sources concerning the possible setting-up of a camp site, at around 9 p.m. on 5 May 2012 he arrived at Bolotnaya Square and organised a search of the area including the park, and the park was cordoned off and guarded.

Zdorenko testified that if necessary, at the decision of the operational headquarters, the venue allocated for the meeting could have been significantly extended by opening up the park at Bolotnaya Square, but there had been no need for that given that there were no more than 2,500-3,000 persons on Bolotnaya Square.

The witness Ms N. Mirza testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that Police Colonel V. Biryukov had asked her and the Ombudsman to come to Malyy Kamennyy Bridge where some of the protesters, including Mr B. Nemtsov and Mr S. Udaltsov, refused to go to the offices of the Moscow Department of the Interior to sign the necessary documents.

The witness Mr D. Gudkov, deputy of the State Duma, testified in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev that together with Mr G. Gudkov he had conducted negotiations with the police and an agreement had been reached that the cordon at Malyy Kamennyy Bridge would be moved back and access to the park would be opened up, but at that point some young men in hoodies among the protesters began pushing citizens onto the cordon, after which the cordon broke, the police began the arrests and mass disorder ensued.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev rejected testimonies to the effect that it was the police who had begun moving towards the protesters who were peacefully sitting on the ground and thus provoked the breaking of the cordon, and found that it was the protesters who began pushing against the cordon, causing the crowd to panic, which eventually led to the breaking of the cordon and the ensuing mass disorder.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that the location of the sit-in was outside the venue approved by the Moscow authorities for the public event.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that there are no grounds to consider the closure of access to the park of Bolotnaya Square and the placement of a guiding police cordon at the foot of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge to be a provocation, since it was only to indicate the direction and it did not obstruct access to the meeting venue at Bolotnaya Square.

The Moscow City Court in the proceedings against Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev found that the mass disorder organised by Mr S. Udaltsov and others led to the destabilisation of public order and peace in a public place during the conduct of a public event, put a large number of people in danger, and led to considerable psychological tension in the vicinity of Bolotnaya Square in Moscow, accompanied by violence against the police and the destruction of property.
The Moscow City Court sentenced Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev to four and a half years' imprisonment.
On 18 March 2015 the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation upheld the judgment of 24 July 2014 convicting Mr S. Udaltsov and Mr Razvozzhayev, with a number of amendments.

On 18 August 2014 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow examined another Bolotnaya case and found four individuals guilty of participating in mass disorder and committing violent acts against police officers during the demonstration on 6 May 2012.
The four individuals found guilty in the second Bolotnaya case received prison sentences of between two and a half and three and a half years; one of them was released on parole.
The judgment of 18 August 2014 in the second Bolotnaya case was upheld by the Moscow City Court on 27 November 2014.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant arrived at Bolotnaya Square at around 6 p.m. to take part in the meeting.
The applicant stood in front of the stage on Bolotnaya Embankment, within the area designated as the meeting venue.
According to the applicant, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. the area around him remained peaceful, although there was general confusion.
The applicant claimed that he had not heard any announcement of the termination of the meeting.

The applicant claimed that he had heard the police orders made through a megaphone to disperse, but in the general commotion he was unable to leave immediately and remained within the authorised meeting area until 7 p.m., when he was arbitrarily arrested by the police dispersing the demonstration.
The applicant denied that he had received any warning or orders before being arrested.
The police apprehended the applicant and took him to a police van, where he waited for an hour before it left Bolotnaya Square for the police station.
According to the applicant, there was no traffic at Bolotnaya Square at the time of his arrest; it was still suspended.
According to the Government, the applicant was arrested at 8.30 p.m. at Bolotnaya Square because he was obstructing the traffic and had disregarded the police order to move away.
At 9.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the applicant was taken to the Krasnoselskiy district police station in Moscow.

At the Krasnoselskiy district police station an on-duty officer drew up a statement on an administrative offence on the basis of a report by Police Officer Y., who had allegedly arrested the applicant.
Police Officer Y.'s report contained a handwritten statement that on 6 May 2012 at 9.30 p.m., at 5/16 Bolotnaya Square, together with Police Lieutenant A., he arrested the applicant (Mr Frumkin).

The rest of Police Officer Y.'s report was a printed template stating that the applicant, acting in a group of citizens, took part in an authorised meeting, went out onto the road and thus obstructed the traffic, did not react to the multiple demands of the police to vacate the road, thereby disobeying a lawful order of the police, who were fulfilling their service duty of maintaining public order and ensuring safety, and thereby committed an administrative offence under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The statement on the administrative offence contained an identical text to the printed template but indicated that the applicant had been arrested at 8.30 p.m.
The applicant was charged with obstructing traffic and disobeying lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant's administrative detention was ordered with reference to Article 27.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The 'reasons' section of the administrative detention order remained blank.
At 2 p.m. on 7 May 2012 the applicant was taken to court, but his case was not examined.
Having spent the day in a transit van without food or drink, at 11.55 p.m. on 7 May 2012 the applicant was taken back to the cell at the Krasnoselskiy district police station.
A new order for the applicant's administrative detention was issued on 7 May 2012, indicating that he had been detained 'for the purpose of drawing up the administrative material'.
At 8 a.m. on 8 May 2012 the applicant was brought before the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka district, who examined the charges.
The applicant requested that the case be adjourned on the grounds that he was unfit to stand trial after the detention; this request was rejected in order to expedite the proceedings.
The applicant requested that the hearing be opened to the public; this request was rejected in order to expedite the proceedings.
The applicant requested that two police officers be examined as witnesses; this request was rejected in order to expedite the proceedings.
A further request by the applicant for the examination of several eyewitnesses was partly refused and partly granted, and three witnesses for the defence were examined.

On the basis of the report written by Police Officer Y., the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka district established that at 8.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the applicant had been walking along the road at Bolotnaya Square and obstructing the traffic, and that he had then disobeyed lawful police orders to vacate the venue.
The Justice of the Peace rejected as unreliable two eyewitnesses' testimonies to the effect that the police had not given the applicant any orders or warnings before arresting him.

The applicant was found guilty of disobeying lawful police orders and was sentenced under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation to fifteen days' administrative detention.
On 11 May 2012 the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow examined an appeal lodged by the applicant.
At the applicant's request the Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow examined Ms S. as a witness on appeal.
Ms S. testified that at 7.46 p.m. on 6 May 2012 she had been looking for her son when she saw the applicant in a police van and spoke to him.
Ms S. testified that at 9.03 p.m. on 6 May 2012 she had been at Bolotnaya Square; the site had been fully cordoned off and the traffic had not resumed.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow rejected the applicant's argument that the police report and the police statement were inconsistent as regards the time of his arrest, finding that the correct interpretation was that the time of arrest had been 8.30 p.m. and the detention at the police station 9.30 p.m.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow dismissed the video-recording submitted by the applicant on the ground that it did not contain the date and the time of the incident, but found that the applicant's guilt had been proved by other evidence.
The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow upheld the first-instance judgment convicting the applicant of disobeying lawful police orders.
On 11 January 2013 the Deputy President of the Moscow City Court examined the applicant's administrative case in supervisory-review proceedings and upheld the earlier judicial decisions.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly adopted by the Venice Commission at its 83rd Plenary Session (Venice, 4 June 2010) provided that an assembly should be deemed peaceful if its organisers have professed peaceful intentions and the conduct of the assembly is non-violent, and that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties.

The Venice Commission Guidelines recommended that wherever possible, and especially in the case of large assemblies or assemblies on controversial issues, the organiser should discuss with the law enforcement officials the security and public safety measures prior to the event.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if a standoff or other dispute arises during the course of an assembly, negotiation or mediated dialogue may be an appropriate means of trying to reach an acceptable resolution.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that any prior restrictions should be formalised in writing and communicated to the organiser of the event within a reasonable timeframe, and that the relevant authorities must ensure that any restrictions imposed during an event are in full conformity with the law.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that resort to hate speech by participants in an assembly does not of itself necessarily justify the dispersal of the event, and law enforcement officials should take measures only against the particular individuals involved.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that no additional restrictions should be imposed by law enforcement personnel during an assembly unless absolutely necessary in light of demonstrably changed circumstances, and that the detention of participants during an assembly should meet a high threshold and should be used only in the most pressing situations when failure to detain would result in the commission of serious criminal offences.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that the regulatory authority should fairly and objectively assess all available information to determine whether the organisers and participants of a notified assembly are likely to conduct the event in a peaceful manner, and should ensure that any relevant concerns raised are communicated to the event organiser with an opportunity to respond.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that any restrictions placed on an assembly should be communicated in writing to the event organiser with a brief explanation of the reason for each restriction, and that such decisions should be communicated within a reasonable timeframe sufficiently far in advance to allow judicial appeal before the notified date of the event.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that governments must ensure that law enforcement officials receive adequate training in the policing of public assemblies, including soft skills such as negotiation and mediation.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement agencies should be proactive in engaging with assembly organizers, that there should be a nominated point of contact within the law enforcement agency whom protesters can contact before or during an assembly, and that the policing operation should be characterized by a policy of 'no surprises'.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement officials should differentiate between peaceful and non-peaceful participants, and that neither isolated incidents of sporadic violence nor the violent acts of some participants are themselves sufficient grounds to impose sweeping restrictions on peaceful participants in an assembly.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that so long as assemblies remain peaceful, they should not be dispersed by law enforcement officials, and that dispersal of assemblies should be a measure of last resort.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that dispersal should not occur unless law enforcement officials have taken all reasonable measures to facilitate and protect the assembly from harm and unless there is an imminent threat of violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if dispersal is deemed necessary, the assembly organiser and participants should be clearly and audibly informed prior to any intervention by law enforcement personnel, and participants should be given reasonable time to disperse voluntarily before law enforcement officials intervene further.
On 4 May 2012 the deputy mayor of Moscow, Mr A. Gorbenko, instructed the Tsentralnyy district prefect to assist the organisers in maintaining public order and security during the event.

On 4 May 2012 the deputy mayor of Moscow, Mr A. Gorbenko, ordered the Moscow Department of Regional Security to inform the organisers that their assembly notice had been accepted and to monitor its implementation.
Other public agencies were assigned the duties of street cleaning, traffic control and ensuring the presence of ambulances at the site of the assembly on 6 May 2012.
On 5 May 2012 the Police Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Golovanov, adopted a plan for safeguarding public order in Moscow on 6 May 2012 (the security plan).

The security plan provided for security measures in Moscow city centre in view of the forthcoming authorised demonstration at Bolotnaya Square and anticipated attempts by other opposition groups to hold unauthorised public gatherings.
The security plan set up operational headquarters to implement the security measures.
Thirty-two high-ranking police officers, including eight major-generals, two military commanders and one emergency-relief official, were appointed to the operational headquarters.
The Deputy Police Chief of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Kozlov, was appointed as head of the operational headquarters.
The Chief of the Special-Purpose Operational Centre of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Khaustov, was appointed as deputy head of the operational headquarters.
The Deputy Chief of the Public Order Directorate of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Colonel D. Deynichenko, was appointed as deputy head of the operational headquarters.

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.
The main contingent of the security plan was the police squad charged with cordon and riot-control duties in accordance with a structured and detailed action plan for each operational unit.

The security plan provided for a 785-strong police unit assigned to operational posts across the city centre, with responsibility for apprehending offenders, escorting them to police stations and drawing up administrative-offence reports.
The 785-strong police unit was instructed to prepare templates for the administrative-offence reports and to have at least forty printed copies of them at every police station.
The security plan provided for a 350-strong police unit for intercepting and apprehending organisers and instigators of unauthorised gatherings.
The 350-strong police unit had to be equipped with full protection gear and police batons.
Each unit in the security plan had to ensure effective radio communication within the chain of command.
Units were instructed to keep loudspeakers, metal detectors, handcuffs, fire extinguishers and wire clippers in the police vehicles.

The security plan set out in detail the allocation and deployment of police vehicles, police buses, interception and monitoring vehicles and equipment, dog-handling teams, fire-fighting and rescue equipment, ambulances and a helicopter.

The security plan made provision for a 1,815-strong reserve unit equipped with gas masks, aerosol grenades (Дрейф), flash grenades (Заря-2), bang grenades (Факел and Факел-C), a 40-mm hand-held grenade launcher (Гвоздь 6Г-30), and a 43-mm hand-held grenade launcher (ГМ-94).
The 1,815-strong reserve unit was also equipped with tubeless pistols (ПБ-4СП) with 23-mm rubber bullets and propelling cartridges, and rifles (KC-23).
Two water-cannon vehicles were ordered to be on standby, ready to be used against persistent offenders.

All units were instructed to be vigilant and thorough in detecting and eliminating security threats and to be polite and tactful in their conduct vis-à-vis citizens, engaging in lawful dialogue with them without responding to provocations.
If faced with an unauthorised gathering, units were instructed to give a warning through a loudspeaker, to arrest the most active participants and to record video-footage of those incidents.

Police chiefs were instructed to place plain-clothes officers among the protesters in order to monitor the threat of violence and terrorist attacks within the crowd and to take measures, where appropriate, to prevent and mitigate the damage and to pursue the perpetrators.

The Chief of the Tsentralnyy district of Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Major-General V. Paukov, was required to prepare, together with the organisers, the text of the public announcement to be made if the situation deteriorated.
The head of the press communication service of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Internal Service Lieutenant-Colonel Y. Alekseyeva, was in charge of communication with the press.

The head of the Department for Liaison with Civil Society of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Internal Service Colonel V. Biryukov, had to ensure coordination with the representatives of public organisations and coordination and information flow with other services of the Moscow Department of the Interior.
The units assigned to police the march and the meeting belonged to Zone no. 8, covering Kaluzhskaya Square, Bolotnaya Square and the adjacent territory.
The zone commander of Zone no. 8 was the Chief of the Riot Police of the Moscow Department of the Interior, Police Colonel P. Smirnov.

Police Colonels P. Saprykin, Y. Zdorenko, A. Kuznetsov, V. Yermakov, A. Kasatkin, A. Dvoynos, Police Lieutenant-Colonel A. Tsukernik, Police Captain R. Bautdinov and Internal Service Lieutenant-Colonel D. Bystrikov were appointed as deputy commanders of Zone no. 8.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 comprised 2,400 riot police officers, of whom 1,158 were on duty at Bolotnaya Square.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to search the demonstrators to prevent them from taking camping tents to the site of the meeting.
The units assigned to Zone no. 8 were instructed to obstruct access to Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, diverting the marchers to Bolotnaya Embankment, the site of the meeting.
The adjacent park at Bolotnaya Square had to be cordoned off under the security plan.

Further arrangements were made for access of the press to the meeting venue.

The command of Zone no. 8, in particular Police Colonels Smirnov and Saprykin, were under orders to meet the organisers in person at the beginning of the event to remind them of their responsibilities and to have them sign an undertaking.

The organisers were to undertake to ensure the lawful and safe conduct of the event, and to refrain from any calls for forced change of the constitutional order and from hate speech and propaganda in favour of violence or war.
The organisers were to undertake to be present at the venue until the end of the assembly and the departure of the participants.
A video-recording of the briefing and the signing of the undertaking had to be made.
At approximately 1.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the organisers were allowed access to Bolotnaya Square to set up the stage and sound equipment.
The police searched the vehicles delivering the equipment and seized three tents found amid the gear.
The police arrested several people for bringing the tents to Bolotnaya Square on 6 May 2012.
The installation of the stage and sound equipment was delayed due to the police searches and arrests.

At the beginning of the march, Police Colonel A. Makhonin met the organisers at Kaluzhskaya Square to clarify any outstanding organisational matters and to have them sign the undertaking to ensure public order during the demonstration.
